sections.title: Can you hear me? Language, Identity, and Power
sections.description:
Why do some ways of speaking sound “educated,” “foreign,” “old,” “authentic”, “professional,” or “deficient”? Who decides where a language ends and a dialect begins? And why are some speakers heard, believed, or treated as authoritative while others are not?
This seminar starts with the following proposition: Language is not only something we use for communication; it is also something we use to act in the world. Through language, we form relationships, express identities, and make judgments about the people around us.. The categories we use—language, dialect, accent, mother tongue, native speaker, standard language—can feel natural, yet they are shaped by histories, institutions, cultural beliefs, and everyday acts of listening. We then explore how ideas about language intersect with race, class, age, gender, and multilingualism in different social and cultural contexts. In the final part of the course, we shift attention from speakers to listeners: How do expectations about a speaker influence what listeners think they hear? When do judgments about language become judgments about a speaker’s personhood?
We investigate these questions through memoir, documentary, film, comedy, podcasts, social media, and scholarship from sociolinguistics, linguistic anthropology, cultural studies, and philosophy. Trevor Noah’s account of moving among languages in apartheid South Africa opens questions about multilingualism and belonging; Betsy Rymes’s work on citizen sociolinguistics helps us analyze ordinary people’s observations and judgments about language; Rosina Lippi-Green examines ideologies of standard language and accent; Nelson Flores and Jonathan Rosa shift attention from the supposedly deficient speaker to the listener; and Miranda Fricker provides a framework for considering how social prejudice can affect a speaker’s credibility as a knower.
